To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

poor service engagement and poor coping style, as well older age and younger onset, are associated with greater symptom severity and poor social functioning, while higher resilience and higher education are associated with better social functioning only, and poor problem-focused coping and higher internalized stigma, together with male gender and depression are associated with symptom severity only.

poor service engagement, poor recovery style, older age, and younger age of onset are related to greater symptomatology; higher education is related to better social function; poor problem-focused coping, internalized stigma, and male gender are related to symptom severity.

poor service engagement, poor recovery style, older age and younger onset, and poor problem-focused coping, internalized stigma, and depression are associated with symptom severity, whereas poor service engagement, younger onset, and depression are linked with poor social functioning.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying the relationships between personal resources, symptom severity and psychsocial functioning in people with schizophrenia.

the relationships of personal resources (i.e., coping strategies, social support, resilience, self-stigma, recovery style, and service engagement) with symptom severity and social functioning in a large sample (n = 921) of people with schizophrenia.
the identification of those personal resources that are most likely to be associated with symptom severity or social functioning in a large sample.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the more the patient has the following resources, the better the patient's outcome: (1) a good service engagement, (2) a good recovery style, (3) a good problem-focused coping, (4) a good resilience, (5) a good education, (6) no male gender, (7) no depression, (8) no internalized stigma, (9) an older age, and (10) a younger age at onset.

the personal resources that are related to better functioning and/or symptom severity are: (1) resilience; (2) problem-focused coping; (3) internalized stigma; (4) education; (5) recovery style; (6) service engagement.
the personal resources that are related to symptom severity and/or psychosocial functioning are not the same.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
personal resources are important for the clinical management of patients with schizophrenia, and that they should be taken into account in the assessment and treatment process.

, in addition to the usual clinical variables, a set of personal resources should be assessed to identify patients with schizophrenia at risk for poor psychosocial functioning or poor symptom severity.

the personal resources of patients with schizophrenia, such as coping style, resilience, internalized stigma and service engagement, may be important factors to be considered in the treatment and care of patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
personal resources may have a role in improving the quality of life of people with schizophrenia, but this role is not always clear.
the relationships of personal resources to symptom severity and psychsocial functioning in schizophrenia are complex and deserve further study.
the relationship between personal resources and symptom severity or psychsocial functioning is more complex than previously thought.
